name: Moritz Seibert
one_paragraph: Moritz Seibert is a practitioner of long-term, commodity-heavy trend following (he runs his own CTA, captioned Takahe/Takahi) who also hosts Open Interest and sometimes Systematic Investor. He believes the money comes from applying a weak, simple entry signal (about 70% of trades lose) to as many truly independent markets as possible, keeping every loss small, and letting rare outliers pay; entry details matter little, initial size and exits matter most. He rejects dynamic resizing (calling it hidden mean reversion that trims winners and cuts the right tail), uses next-settlement execution with no resting stops, avoids overfitting and never tweaks the system after a drawdown. He treats costs and execution as first-order (a high-turnover futures strategy faces roughly a 10% a year hurdle), thinks calendar and flow effects tied to human schedules persist while published or crowded effects decay, and sees trend as a non-equity-beta stream that deserves a performance fee while industry volatility has halved and fees have not. Much of his material is questions to guests, so many of his views are stated briefly and without data.

core_beliefs.belief: Trend following needs no forecast. The entry signal is weak (about 70% of trades lose, 30% win); profits come from a few outliers and from keeping losses small. Entry details matter little for a long-term system, and the trend follower's edge is enduring bad periods ('pain arbitrage').
core_beliefs.stable: stable - same risk-first logic in 2024 (MT020, accepting Eckhardt's frame) and 2025 (MT207 own statistics).

core_beliefs.belief: Apply the small edge to as many genuinely independent return streams as possible (small, alternative and venue-split markets: Chinese futures, canola, lumber, livestock, regional carbon, COMEX vs LME copper, London vs New York sugar). Independence, not market count, is the target; capacity is capped near USD 500m because small markets cannot absorb billions.
core_beliefs.stable: stable - 2024 (MT020, MT201 leading questions) to 2026 (MT130: hindsight ranking of concentrated vs broad says nothing about the future). He concedes smaller portfolios can outperform for periods (MT020-C10-2).

core_beliefs.belief: Do not resize a position after entry. Vol- or risk-based resizing trims winners, makes a trend system behave like mean reversion with extra costs, and cuts the right tail (gold, livestock 2025). Initial sizing and initial stop room are the main risk control. After a drawdown size on current closed-trade equity (1m to 500k, not 250k) without extra de-risking.
core_beliefs.stable: stable - first as a question in MT020 (resizing is a hidden mean-reversion trade, 'more often than not'), stated flat in MT207. He admits it is 'a question of taste' with a smoother-return alternative.

core_beliefs.belief: Keep rules simple and robust; extra filters and parameters improve backtests, not future returns. Never change the system after a drawdown (SVB, dollar-yen, April 2025); be wary of new risk-premium indices that are small twists on existing ones.

Costs and execution are first-order. A short-term futures strategy faces about 5-6 dollars all-in per contract and about 10% a year in execution cost at ~8,000 round turns per million. In a direct CTA slippage lands on client P&L, so market-by-market execution research and patient execution have value.
core_beliefs.stable: stable (see internal tension on the size of the cost drag).

core_beliefs.belief: Flow and calendar effects tied to human schedules and accounting (month-end, vol-control and risk-parity rebalancing) persist; effects that are published, crowded or allocation-driven (commodity index roll days 5-9) decay. Crowding charges against trend have recurred for decades, so they should be tested, not assumed, yet too much money in a niche does erode returns.
core_beliefs.stable: stable, with a qualifier: crowding is both 'test it' and 'textbook decay'.

core_beliefs.belief: Short-term systems have suffered alpha decay; long-term systems (about 200-day look-backs) remain robust. System speed decides outcomes around sharp turns (2025 trend dispersion of about 10% tied to speed around the April V-shape).
core_beliefs.stable: stable - compatible; the second claim is offered without data ('not that I have too much data').

core_beliefs.belief: Trend is a return stream with no equity-like drift (commodities should be traded long and short) and is not equity beta, so it deserves a performance fee; fund volatility has roughly halved with size and allocator career risk while fees did not fall, and cheap replicators form a benchmark that performance-fee managers must beat. Trend and long-short are wrongly benchmarked to the S&P 500, and the CTA index (largest 20 managers) hides alternative-market managers.
core_beliefs.stable: stable. He calls the fee explanation a hypothesis ('nobody will have the definitive answer').

core_beliefs.belief: Volatility is not risk to a trend follower, and futures returns are fat-tailed and jump-prone on both sides, so a standard-deviation volatility measure reintroduces normal-distribution assumptions. A trend follower prefers punchy returns in stress events (trend funds running 8-12% vol lack the punch of earlier decades).

Be sceptical of price-prediction machine learning (it would fit noise and rediscover buying breakouts) and of replication portfolios without predefined exits (exposed to gaps); in commodities exchanges and talk-your-book traders distort prices (margin hikes force squeezes, LME nickel trade cancellation bailed out the distressed side).

The 30-40 year edge of long over short trades in equity and bond trend following is a sample-specific effect of secular bull markets; he asks guests whether to bias signals long (Nobow: no, equal long and short keeps crisis alpha).
core_beliefs.stable: stable (only one appearance; the question is also a test of the guests' philosophy).

mechanisms.name: Independent markets to higher risk-adjusted return and a capacity cap
chain: small trend edge per market -> apply it to many independent markets -> add small, uncorrelated markets (Chinese futures, canola, lumber, livestock, regional carbon) -> fund capped near USD 500m
mechanisms.fails_when: A large correlated shock (Liberation Day, tariffs) puts positions on in many markets at once, so more markets with positions means a bigger single-day loss; he does not force positions in every market.

mechanisms.name: Weak entry, small losses, outlier-driven profit
chain: entry signal poor (about 70% losers) -> entry details matter little for a long-term system -> profit depends on initial size, stop room and give-back exit -> losses stay small and rare outliers pay -> less volatility drag and easier recovery from drawdowns
mechanisms.fails_when: A manager may not stay with the system through wild single-month swings (behavioural risk, not a model failure).

mechanisms.name: Why resizing is rejected
chain: price moves in the trader's favour or volatility rises -> vol- or risk-based sizing trims the winner -> trend system behaves like mean reversion with extra commissions and bid-offer -> lower asymmetry and fewer right-tail years, smoother returns and smaller drawdowns
mechanisms.fails_when: Event risk: a no-resizing position can be stopped out by a one- or two-day move and give-back potential is larger (Niels's counter); he calls the choice a matter of taste.

mechanisms.name: Delayed next-settlement execution instead of resting stops
chain: signal from last settlement -> trade at next day's settlement, no stop orders -> not picked off and not stopped by flash spikes (South African rand) -> slightly better overall returns than stops in own tests
mechanisms.fails_when: Overnight gaps: a COMEX copper long exited near 4.6 versus a theoretical exit above 5.17 after a tariff announcement.

mechanisms.name: Cost hurdle for high-turnover systems
chain: about 8,000 round turns per million at about 6 dollars a contract -> roughly 10% a year execution drag -> pre-cost risk-adjusted return must be very high to net a profit
mechanisms.fails_when: Per-contract costs or turnover are lower than assumed (Vishal says performance is not highly sensitive; his own arithmetic does not fully reconcile: 8,000 x 2 x $6 is about 9.6%).

mechanisms.name: Execution slippage in a CTA versus a QIS
chain: QIS index documentation guarantees a settlement price -> slippage sits on the bank's book; direct CTA trading -> slippage hits client P&L -> patient, market-specific execution in small markets gives near-nil slippage instead of 2-3% a year
mechanisms.fails_when: Not stated; evidence is a second-hand Gresham report.

mechanisms.name: Human-schedule flows versus decaying crowded effects
chain: calendar-based processes of humans and big capital pools -> predictable month-end flows that persist despite publication; risk-parity and vol-control funds must cut exposure as prices fall and volatility rises -> exploitable selling for a few days; index roll window -> liquidity premium that decayed once investors spread rolls
mechanisms.fails_when: Decays once participants adapt (roll premium); he says too much money chasing a niche decays it but does not know.

mechanisms.name: System speed around the April 2025 V-shape
chain: April equity sell-off then recovery -> fast systems capture the V, medium speed whipsawed, slow systems stopped out to flat -> long-term system re-enters only in July-August -> about 10% of 2025 trend dispersion
mechanisms.fails_when: Not tested on data ('not that I have too much data to support it').

mechanisms.name: Industry volatility, allocators and fees
chain: large AUM -> lower volatility target (halving vol halves contracts, cutting impact and slippage) -> institutional tickets and allocator career risk push funds to cut vol -> fees not cut commensurately -> asset-based management fee dominates, asset-gathering mode, weaker alignment
mechanisms.fails_when: Offered explicitly as unproven; Niels disputes it (flat fees, ETF replicators below 1%).

mechanisms.name: Fee compression from cheap replication
chain: cheap replication ETFs deliver trend beta -> performance-fee hedge funds must beat them -> squeeze on generic trend managers

mechanisms.name: Exchange margin hikes and interventions
chain: exchange raises margin near highs (ICE cocoa) -> shorts forced to cover -> squeeze higher; exchange cancels trades in a squeeze (LME nickel 2022) -> protects clearing house but bails out the distressed side

playbook.rule: Derivative-free entries: price versus price N days ago, new 200-day (also 100-day) high; moving averages avoided though they also work. Signal is taken from the last settlement.
playbook.why: Simplicity and robustness; a new high improves on random entry.

playbook.rule: Add markets for independence (Chinese futures, canola, lumber, livestock, regional carbon); trade COMEX and LME, London and New York versions separately and split risk; skip very small emerging carbon markets that are hard to access; trade long and short; keep a broad universe including alternatives even in an energy/metals-led year.
playbook.why: Maximise independent streams; access and operational risk limit the universe, not weak trend properties.

playbook.rule: Initial position size and stop room are the control; no resizing for volatility or heat afterwards; no forced position in every market; after a drawdown size on current closed-trade equity with no extra reduction.
playbook.why: Later resizing is profit-taking; extra de-risking leaves too little risk to recover and distorts system statistics; open-trade equity invites over-risking.

playbook.rule: Keep losses small with an initial stop and a give-back exit; exits go to flat (no forced reversal to short); do not change the system after a drawdown.
playbook.why: Volatility drag makes deep drawdowns hard to recover from; neutral zone avoids reversing into whipsaws.

playbook.rule: Trade at the next day's settlement; no resting stops, entry or exit; use broker-based execution in brokered markets (CCAs, South African grains); execute market by market and invest in execution research.
playbook.why: Avoid stop picking and spike glitches; slightly better returns than stops in own tests; broker execution may beat hitting screen quotes at a cost of a penny; slippage lands on client P&L.

playbook.rule: Cap fund capacity near USD 500m (a moving target); the long-term fund holds trends for years (orange juice over two years, short Henry Hub over two years, earning roll yield in contango).
playbook.why: Keep a meaningful footprint in small markets; slow trend followers need little liquidity.

playbook.rule: Searches for entry improvements found nothing statistically better than a new high; question new indices that are minor twists on old ones; test crowding claims rather than assume them.
playbook.why: Cutting losers from 70% to 60% would lift returns sharply but no signal does; launch pressure and over-optimisation.

playbook.rule: No asset-based management fee; performance fee only.

evidence_style: Mostly interviewer questions, back-of-envelope arithmetic (cost hurdle), first principles and analogies (casino tables, Occam's razor), own fund experience and results (2025-2026 P&L attribution), industry index data read at the start of shows, and second-hand reports of other managers. Describes internal tests (delayed execution versus stops, entry research) without showing numbers. Sceptical of unproven claims, but asserts several things himself without data (fee explanation, vol-halving research shared only selectively, trend speed effect).

views_timeline.view: Short-term trend systems show alpha decay while 200-day-type systems remain robust.
views_timeline.reasoning: Turtle students and diversified trend followers moved to longer holding periods.

views_timeline.view: The transaction-cost hurdle for a high-turnover intraday futures strategy is roughly 10% a year, so the strategy must be extremely accurate.
views_timeline.reasoning: About 8,000 round turns per million and about $6 per contract.

views_timeline.view: His trend fund's short Henry Hub position (more than two years) was closed by the late-February 2025 rally.
views_timeline.reasoning: Colder weather outlook triggered a reversal.

views_timeline.view: CTA space in a drawdown (equities and trend both falling); hopes it is early innings and that trend recovers within 30-50 days.

Long livestock (lean hogs, live and feeder cattle), precious metals (platinum, silver, gold) and cocoa; coffee re-entered long after a whipsaw; underexposed to fixed income; losses YTD in currencies, equities and bonds since April; long-end yields rising on fiscal concern.
views_timeline.reasoning: Systems in strong uptrends and not reversed; stopped out in April; bond markets judged rangebound; debt-to-GDP reasoning (Japan above 200%).

views_timeline.view: S&P +18% YTD and MSCI World +22% decoupled from CTA indices (BTop50 +2.35%, trend about flat, short-term traders -4.6%); October trend gains in precious metals and livestock gave back after about 20 October; rates were the main 2025 whipsaw, currencies second worst, equities the only clearly positive sector; his long-term system exited almost all equity markets in April and re-entered July-August.

Trend following is doing well in 2026 amid large volatility, especially petroleum (BTOP50 above 11% YTD, SG CTA about 12%, short-term traders +6%, S&P 500 TR +9%); Brent/WTI backwardation could widen in a supply crisis; a SpaceX IPO would raise S&P concentration; doubts the WSJ claim that QIS revenue is nearly risk-free (QIS about $1 trillion, $3 trillion levered).
views_timeline.reasoning: Index data, a conversation with a Middle East oil trader, quoted article.

how_views_changed: Methodology did not change between mid-2024 and mid-2026: small losses, simple entries, no resizing, independent markets, careful execution. Only market positioning changed (short Henry Hub closed Feb 2025, long-term equity exposure stopped out in April 2025 and rebuilt in July-August, metals/livestock long in autumn 2025, petroleum-led trend gains in 2026). He explicitly says not to tweak the system after drawdowns. No explained revision of a belief.

disagreements.topic: Bias signals toward long in equities and bonds given 30-40 years of data?
disagreements.their_position: Notes long trades beat short and asks whether to tilt.
disagreements.other_position: Nobow: equal risk in long and short; tilting to the past is overfitting and kills crisis alpha. Valin: some CTAs do bias, a source of dispersion.

disagreements.their_position: Resizing to rising volatility is a hidden mean-reversion trade; standard-deviation vol reintroduces normality; maximum diversification with more independent bets.
disagreements.other_position: Santino: ETC keeps sizes constant and does not target vol. Eckhardt: alternative markets look better on paper but are worse in practice because of slippage and exit difficulty; trades about 70 markets.

disagreements.topic: Should a non-trend book add trend; do patterns decay?
disagreements.their_position: Adding trend would probably still raise risk-adjusted return; month-end effects are sticky unlike published anomalies.
disagreements.other_position: Optimal blend is the allocator's job; non-stationarity is not universal and patterns should be judged individually.

disagreements.topic: Cost hurdle for short-term trading; benchmark
disagreements.their_position: About 10% a year in execution cost; asks if J8 should be benchmarked against multi-strategy funds.
disagreements.other_position: Vishal: performance is not highly sensitive to small cost changes. Tilman: CTA universe is essentially a diversified 12-month momentum portfolio; J8 is about 50% CTA, 50% alternative risk premia.

disagreements.their_position: A machine would learn noise and rediscover breakouts; his fund holds trends for years and earns roll yield.
disagreements.other_position: Never ML for entry, only for post-entry exits; 2-5 day holds, ignores curves.

disagreements.topic: Long tail of markets; recalibration of a fixed fit
disagreements.their_position: Likes fat-tail and alternative markets, spreads and punchy returns; a fixed bottom-up fit has no response function if managers change.
disagreements.other_position: Hoffstein: longer tail raises Sharpe but weakens crisis offset; annual reruns will not change weights meaningfully. Butler: weights and speeds stable in cross-validation.

disagreements.topic: Dynamic sizing, fees, moving averages, investor interest
disagreements.their_position: No resizing; fees did not fall with volatility; derivative-free entries; investors care about net performance.
disagreements.other_position: No resizing leaves event risk; CTA fee pressure is real; large managers may use moving averages; institutions want process detail.

disagreements.topic: QIS size and why the roll congestion trade flattened
disagreements.their_position: Takes the $1.3tn figure with delta/double-counting caveats; crowding may have removed the roll premium.
disagreements.other_position: Figure uncertain both ways; flat not negative, so an elastic market rather than QIS crowding; trend may benefit from early crowding.

disagreements.topic: Execution value, WSJ framing of QIS, broad versus concentrated universe
disagreements.their_position: In a CTA slippage flows to client so execution research has value; doubts QIS revenue is near risk-free; concentrated metals/energy CTAs did 50-100% in 2026 but that is hindsight.
disagreements.other_position: No execution alpha for the client in QIS; crowding is time variation for true premia; core universe for defensiveness, broader for long-run Sharpe.

disagreements.topic: Is physical information a durable edge?
disagreements.their_position: A physical business gives an information flow and could be a great advantage.
disagreements.other_position: Useful for conviction and filtering, but the physical trading arm was hard to run and disbanded.

internal_tensions.issue: Wants as many independent markets as possible (more independent bets, less noise), yet notes that more markets with positions means a larger single-day loss in a correlated shock (Liberation Day) and that hindsight ranking of broad versus concentrated says nothing about the future.

Says the entry signal is poor and entry details matter little, yet reports own research that a new 100/200-day high improves on random entry and that cutting the loser rate from 70% to 60% would lift returns sharply.

Execution cost is described as an extreme hurdle (about 10% a year, an arithmetic that does not fully reconcile) for short-term trading, but also as nearly eliminable (near-nil slippage versus 2-3% a year) with patient, researched execution in his own style.
Crowding: charges against trend should be tested, not assumed (trend persists for decades), but too much money in a niche decays its returns and the roll-window premium decayed.
No resting stops and delayed execution are preferred and said to be slightly better, yet the copper long exited near 4.6 versus a theoretical 5.17 after an overnight tariff gap.
Expects month-end and vol-control footprints to be exploitable while rejecting the same vol-based resizing in his own book as mean reversion.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: A long-term trend system entering on a new 100/200-day high beats random entry with the same exit and sizing, win rate about 30%, and no tested alternative entry beats a new high.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Daily futures series for a broad universe; random-entry Monte Carlo with identical exits.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Executing at the next day's settlement with no resting stops gives slightly better returns than stop orders across systems and markets, with the exception of overnight gap events.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Settlement and intraday prices; the same signals run with stop versus delayed exits.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: A trend portfolio without post-entry volatility or heat resizing has higher skew, right-tail years and net return (after commissions and bid-offer) than the same portfolio with vol-based resizing, at the cost of larger drawdowns.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Trend backtest with and without resizing; transaction cost model; skew and drawdown statistics.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Adding small, genuinely independent markets (Chinese futures, canola, lumber, livestock, regional carbon) and venue-split commodities (COMEX vs LME, London vs New York) raises the risk-adjusted return of a trend portfolio; regional carbon markets are mutually uncorrelated.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Return correlations and incremental Sharpe of small markets; capacity estimates.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: A short-term futures strategy at about 8,000 round turns per million and about $6 per contract loses roughly 10% a year to execution cost, so only very accurate systems net a profit.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Cost per contract by market; turnover and net-of-cost Sharpe of short-term CTA indices.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Month-end effects persist because of human schedules, while the commodity index roll window (business days 5-9) premium has largely decayed.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Monthly seasonality in futures and equities by sample era; roll-window returns of GSCI/DJ-UBS.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Risk-parity and vol-control funds create selling flow for a few days after prices fall and volatility rises, which is exploitable.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Modelled vol-control exposure changes against subsequent short-horizon returns.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Faster trend systems outperformed slower ones in 2025 by about 10% around the April V-shape; long-term systems exited equity in April and re-entered only in July-August.
Over 30-40 years, long trend trades in equity and bonds beat short trades while currencies and commodities differ, a sample-specific effect of secular bull markets.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Long-only and short-only trend returns by asset class, split by sub-period.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Hedge-fund rolling 12-month realized volatility has roughly halved while fees did not fall (multistrategy fees rose).
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Hedge fund database volatility and fee terms by year.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Sizing on closed-trade equity and not cutting further after a drawdown (1m to 500k, not 250k) recovers faster and preserves system statistics than additional de-risking.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Backtest of sizing rules after drawdowns; recovery time.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Patient, market-specific execution in small markets reduces CTA slippage to near nil versus 2-3% a year without careful execution.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Implementation shortfall by market and execution style.

blind_spots: (reader) Gives no numbers for his own fund's costs, win rate by market, Sharpe, drawdown or capacity; his tests are described but not shown.
(reader) Never quantifies the correlation between supposedly independent small markets or how correlation rises in stress, beyond the Liberation Day anecdote.
(reader) No model of what drives commodity trends (fundamentals, macro regimes) beyond a few examples; macro statements (fiscal pressure on long yields, SpaceX concentration) are brief asides.
(reader) The exit rule (initial stop room, give-back) is never specified numerically, so the playbook cannot be replicated.
(reader) The fee/allocator-career-risk explanation of falling volatility is an unproven hypothesis he states firmly; the claim that vol roughly halved rests on unpublished research.
(reader) Little on how to choose look-backs, how many to blend, or why 200-day rather than other horizons.
reader_inferences: (reader) His coherent identity is a convexity-first, outlier-dependent trend follower: low win rate, small losses, no resizing, broad independent universe, simplicity as protection against overfitting.

(reader) His choices cluster around keeping the payoff right-skewed (no resizing, punchy returns in stress, wide universe) at the cost of smoother returns, which is why his critiques of lower-vol, asset-gathering funds are consistent.

(reader) Attribution caution: MT135 merges two co-hosts named Moritz (Seibert and Moritz Heiden); MT204 caption reads 'Morris Seabirds' and MT207 'Moritz' (guest); MT020 claim C13-1 and MT082/MT118 claims were corrected by the pack builder. Claims from MT135 and the guest speaker role in MT207 may mix voices.

(reader) As a host, many 'beliefs' are questions framed as propositions; weight statements with first-person fund evidence (MT207, MT204, MT130) more heavily than interview framing (MT201, MT118, MT108).
